haiku-low.q1: Keys are loaded at startup, before readiness. /healthz returns 503 until all three keys are held, then 200.
haiku-low.q2: It retries 3 times, 2 seconds apart, then logs an error naming the secret and exits with code 1. It never becomes ready, so old pods keep serving live traffic.
haiku-low.q3: A timer re-fetches every 5 minutes and swaps in a changed version, keeping the old one as previous. If the read fails, it keeps the last good value, logs a warning, and retries next tick.
haiku-low.q4: Held in process memory, in small self-redacting objects. Keys must never appear in environment variables, disk, logs (including HTTP debug logs and headers), or the image.
haiku-low.q5: Only the orders-api-prod service identity reads prod values, plus its prod KMS decrypt. Only the security on-call group can write them. Engineers have no prod read or decrypt.
haiku-low.q6: Removing them from the file leaves the live keys valid, and history keeps them. They become harmless only when revoked at the provider in step 10, after all instances use new keys.
haiku-low.q7: Clients read the current key from the secrets module in memory on every call, not copying it at construction. Refresh swaps the in-memory value, so calls pick it up.
haiku-low.q8: Step 8 checks each of the 4 pods: running the recorded image digest, and its latest secret_loaded or secret_rotated log line showing the step 3 version ids. Non-prod and other consumers are checked too.
haiku-low.q9: Set store access (1), write new keys to the store after issuing them at providers (3), change code and remove file keys (5), roll out (7), then revoke old provider keys (10).
haiku-low.q10: make run uses the engineer's own identity to read sandbox or test keys from orders-api/dev. make run-offline uses in-process fake dummy values, never live keys.
haiku-low.q11: It retries the missing secret as part of the 4 total attempts. If still missing after the fourth attempt, it logs an error naming the secret and exits with code 1.
haiku-low.q12: NOT STATED. Security has not decided on scheduled rotation or cadence, and this plan sets none.

sonnet.q1: Keys are loaded into memory at startup, before the instance reports ready. /healthz returns 503 until all three keys are held, then 200.
sonnet.q2: It retries (3 retries, 2s apart, 4 attempts total), then logs an error naming the secret and exits with code 1. It never becomes ready, so with maxUnavailable: 0 the rollout halts and the old pods keep serving with the old, still-valid keys. Live traffic is unaffected.
sonnet.q3: A refresh timer every 5 minutes fetches the latest of each secret. If the version id differs, it swaps in the new value, keeps one previous value, and logs secret_rotated. If the read fails, it keeps the last good value, logs a warning with secret name and error class, retries at the next tick, and readiness is unchanged.
sonnet.q4: Held in process memory, each key in a small object swapped as a whole that redacts itself when printed. Never in environment variables, disk, or logs (including HTTP debug logs and request headers). Only version ids are logged.
sonnet.q5: Read: the orders-api-prod service identity (read on orders-api/prod/* plus decrypt on the prod KMS key). Engineers get no read or decrypt on prod. Write: only the security on-call group.
sonnet.q6: NOT STATED why deletion alone is insufficient in so many words, but the document says git history is not rewritten and the leaked keys remain in it. What makes them harmless is step 10: revoking the old keys at each provider, after which the keys in history are dead. The store holds only new, rotated keys.
sonnet.q7: The secrets module holds the keys in memory. On every call the client asks the secrets module for the current key (a memory read), rather than copying it in __init__. This is so singletons built at import don't keep a stale value.
sonnet.q8: Step 8: for each of the 4 pods (listed from the cluster), confirm it runs the image digest recorded in step 7, and that its latest secret_loaded or secret_rotated log line for each secret shows the version id recorded in step 3. Non-prod deployments and other consumers are also checked. Step 10 also gates on the provider's "last used" for the old key having stopped advancing for at least 15 minutes, and the step 8 check is re-run just before each revocation.
sonnet.q9: Access policy and KMS (step 1, with the step 2 inventory), then issue new keys at the providers and write them to the store (step 3), then dev setup (step 4), code change that switches the app to the store and removes keys from the config file, with the CI guard in the same PR (steps 5 and 6), then merge and roll out (step 7), confirm, bake, then revoke the old keys (steps 8 to 10). Leaked keys are never copied into the store. Keys are rotated at the providers before the app switch, and the old keys are revoked last.
sonnet.q10: make run sets APP_ENV=dev and the app reads orders-api/dev/* from the store using the engineer's own identity, through the same code path as prod. Those hold provider sandbox or test keys, not live keys. make run-offline (APP_ENV=local) uses an in-process fake source with dummy values and stub URLs.
sonnet.q11: A missing secret is treated like an unreachable store: it retries up to 3 times, 2 seconds apart (4 attempts total), then logs an error naming the secret and exits with code 1. It never becomes ready.
sonnet.q12: No. Scheduled rotation is undecided and not planned. The plan sets no cadence. If security decides yes, step 16's mechanism would be used and a cadence and owner added. (The app does refresh from the store every 5 minutes, but that is not rotation.)
